title: Passover
lead: The spring festival that remembers the night the LORD struck Egypt's firstborn and spared Israel's houses marked with blood (Exodus 12). Jews keep it with the Seder meal; Christians see its fulfillment in Jesus, who died at Passover, and call Easter by its name, Pascha.

sections.b: After Exodus 12, the festival is fixed in Israel's calendar on the fourteenth of the first month, followed by seven days of unleavened bread (Leviticus 23:5–8; Deuteronomy 16:1–8). Numbers 9 adds a second Passover a month later for those who were unclean or away. Israel keeps it on entering Canaan at Gilgal (Joshua 5:10–12). Two kings are remembered for great Passovers: Hezekiah, who invited the north (2 Chronicles 30), and Josiah, of whom it is said no such Passover had been kept since the judges (2 Kings 23:21–23; 2 Chronicles 35). The returned exiles keep it at the rebuilt Temple (Ezra 6:19–22). Deuteronomy moves the sacrifice from the home to "the place the LORD will choose."
sections.refs: Leviticus 23:5–8; Numbers 9:1–14; Deuteronomy 16:1–8; Joshua 5:10–12; 2 Kings 23:21–23; 2 Chronicles 30:1–27; 2 Chronicles 35:1–19; Ezra 6:19–22

sections.h: Passover in the Gospels and Paul
sections.b: Jesus goes up to Jerusalem for Passover as a boy (Luke 2:41–42), and John's Gospel is framed by three Passovers (John 2:13; 6:4; 11:55). The Last Supper is set at the feast, with bread and cup given new meaning (Mark 14:12–25; Luke 22:7–20). John has Jesus die when the lambs were slaughtered and notes that none of his bones was broken (John 19:14, 36). Paul calls Christ "our Passover" and urges a feast of sincerity without the old leaven (1 Corinthians 5:7–8). Hebrews 11:28 counts Moses' Passover as an act of faith.
